7d75d9ade537eab2a5c0819ca7cdc0a42e75de0d.answer: Yes, there is a right for a data subject to transmit or receive personal data concerning him or her [Recital 68]. However, this right should not be exercised against controllers processing personal data in the exercise of their public duties, specifically where processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest, the exercise of an official authority vested in the controller, or compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject [Recital 68]. Additionally, this right does not obligate controllers to maintain or adopt processing systems that are technically compatible, and it must be without prejudice to the rights and freedoms of other data subjects [Recital 68].

Yes, you have the right to transmit your personal data to another controller without hindrance from the controller to which the data was provided, provided that:
* The processing is carried out by automated means (Article 20(1)(b), Recital 68); and
* The processing is based on a contract pursuant to point (b) of Article 6(1) or on consent pursuant to point (a) of Article 6(1) or point (a) of Article 9(2) (Article 20(1)(a), Recital 68).

Additionally, where technically feasible, you have the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another (Article 20(2)). 

This right does not apply where processing is based on a legal ground other than consent or contract, nor should it be exercised against controllers processing personal data in the exercise of their public duties (Recital 68).

No, you do not always have to tell affected individuals. Communication to the data subject is not required if:
* The controller has taken subsequent measures ensuring that the high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects is no longer likely to materialise (Article 34(b)); or
* It would involve disproportionate effort, in which case a public communication or similar measure may be used instead to inform data subjects in an equally effective manner (Article 34(c)).

61ee934dbe464aac9d957cb57c7db1e607062f3c.answer: No, you do not always have to tell affected individuals. Communication to the data subject is required when the personal data breach is "likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons" (Article 34(1), Recital 86). Furthermore, communication is not required if the controller has implemented appropriate technical and organisational protection measures that render the affected personal data unintelligible to any unauthorised person, such as encryption (Article 34(3)(a)).
